world.setting: Everyday business and life: rival companies, a beach, a two-lane road, a boardroom, a bank, a hunting ground. Everyman adults, no period costume.
world.register: contemporary everyman; explanatory diagrams and icons over talking heads

lean.name: BB Lean
lean.role: Rival firm executive who undercuts on price to take the whole market
lean.look: Early-40s businessman, average build, short graying hair, navy suit and tie, holding a rolled price sheet

fred.name: Fred
fred.role: Hunter who must choose between a stag and a rabbit with a partner
fred.look: Mid-30s man, slight build, short brown hair, canvas work coat and boots, carrying a hunting bow

end.name: Rainbow's End
end.role: Rival firm executive who must decide whether to hold price or cut it
end.look: Late-50s woman, slight build, silver hair, dark suit jacket over a blouse, holding a folder marked with a price

which.name: Driver

which.look: Late-teens young man, average build, messy dark hair, plain t-shirt and jeans, gripping a steering wheel

road.look: Two-lane dirt road in flat open country, two cars facing each other head-on

office.look: Corporate boardroom with glass walls and a long table, a price chart on the wall

objects.why: The book's central frame: the whole argument is a game with rules and players
Recurring prop for the rival firms' calls and price decisions; a phone is the everyday device of negotiation
Pricing wars and military escalation are the book's recurring stake
Bank runs and trust: coins and money drive the confidence-game examples
Winning the game of chicken and the glory of the one who does not swerve
The head-on road of the chicken game, an existing icon
The cars in the chicken game; the steering wheel removed to commit
The catastrophic head-on outcome both drivers risk
The beach and the warning not to go into the water
Gifts and rewards in the cooperation examples
Burning bridges to make a credible commitment

spine.claim: Strategy is a game: your best move depends on what the other side expects you to do, not on how strong you are.
Commitment and credible threats change the outcome: remove your own choices to win.
Cooperation and trust fail when each player wants the other to move first.
Real people factor in spite, emotion and irrationality, so the model must be adjusted.
Most business conflict is a game where the best move depends on what the other side expects you to do.
